newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sees faster 97 growth, says 12 meet EMU test.
newsitem.headline: EU sees faster 97 growth, says 12 meet EMU test.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday painted a rosy outlook for economic growth in 1997 and saw a vast majority of 12 nations in the European Union meeting the tests for a single currency.
Economic growth in the 15-member EU is now expected to advance at a rate of 1.6 percent in 1996, rising further to 2.3 percent in 1997, the Commission said.

In its twice-yearly review of economic conditions, the EU's executive showed that only Britain, Italy and Greece might not be able to bring their deficits down to no more than 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, a key condition for joining the single currency.
Countries wishing to join the single currency in 1999 must meet a series of economic criteria in 1997, including relatively tight budget policies.

But despite its calculations, the Commission held out the hope that both Italy and Britain could still qualify for membership under the deficit criteria listed for economic and monetary union in the Maastricht treaty agreed in 1991.
It said it was still considering tough budget proposals now before the Italian parliament.
A British budget due to be uneviled later this month could also lead to a revision of the British figures.
The Commission's review coincided with an evaluation by the European Monetary Institute of the progress countries are currently making towards monetary union.

The EMI, the Frankfurt-based forerunner to a European central bank, warned that many European nations -- including Germany, France and Italy -- must make sustained efforts to meet criteria for the single European currency.
It emphasised that budgetary conditions in most countries do not presently meet the criteria for economic and monetary union.
In a separate report on convergence, the Commission also acknowledged that based on 1996 data, only Denmark, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands met the requirements for EMU.
Several economists said the Commission's review was largely predictable given its vested interest in the process.
"Everybody expected them to be extremely optimistic and that is what they were," said Holger Schmeiding, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
But some said the Commission's robust outlook was not so far-fetched given the efforts many governments are making to consolidate their finances.

"The combination of the scope governments have within Maastricht and the policies already announced suggest to us that most of them are going to make it," said Bruce Kasman, chief European economist at J.P. Morgan in London.
On the growth outlook, the Commission's estimates for the EU were little changed from its last forecast in the spring.

At that time, the Commission saw GDP rising at a rate of 1.5 percent in 1996, followed by a 2.4 percent pickup next year. For Germany, the EU's economic powerhouse, economic growth was revised sharply upward in 1996, from 0.5 percent to 1.4 percent.
EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy, speaking at a news conference, said: "The situation is somewhat rosier now than it was in the spring."

While the better economic outlook in Germany contributed greatly to the upbeat assessment for next year, the Commission noted that a slackening in growth in Italy -- from 1.8 percent to 0.8 percent -- held back the overall gain.
"The slowdown in Italy is linked to the appreciation of the lira and to the process of domestic stabilisation," the Commission's report said.
Without the dampening effect of Italy's slower growth, EU GDP growth would be a quarter of percentage point higher in 1996 and 1997.

While Italy's budget deficit was forecast at 3.3 percent of GDP in 1997, the Commission is still investigating whether a further reduction of 0.3 percent is possible under the government's proposed budget.
The scramble to meet EMU preconditions have led nearly all members to engage in some questionable accounting practices.
De Silguy warned that one-off budgetary measures designed to meet the Maastricht criteria would not be tolerated beyond 1997 and stressed the need for durable convergence.

In particular, France's decision to use the proceeds from the privatisation of France Telecom to lower its 1997 budget deficit has prompted a storm of criticism, most notably from German officials who worry about sustainable budgetary rigour.

Yet Germany, often considered a paragon of fiscal virtue, is having its own problems in curbing public expenditure, with Finance Minister Theo Waigel coming under increasing fire for his handling of the government's finances.

While the Commission sees Germany's deficit meeting the three percent GDP threshold, the country's level of public debt is expected to climb above 60 percent of total output this year and next -- a trend at odds with the treaty's preconditons.
